llm_response.content:
Empirical Research Plan – “Early-life Mortality and the 1997 Indonesian Wildfires”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented by an event-study in leads/lags.

Why appropriate?
• The 1997 wildfires produced a sharp, plausibly exogenous jump in ambient particulates that differed markedly across space but occurred at a common point in time.  
• We observe several pre- and post-fire years (e.g., 1994-2000) for the same regions, permitting comparison of mortality trends before and after the shock.  
• DID differences out unobserved, time-invariant regional factors and nation-wide shocks that are common to all regions.  
• An event-study (dynamic DID) lets us test the parallel-trends assumption and trace persistence of health effects.

Continuous (“dose-response”) extension: In most specifications we interact the post-fire dummy with the actual pollution increase, so treatment intensity varies smoothly (Angrist & Pischke 2009 “continuous DID”).  Where necessary we use wildfire exposure (e.g., NASA fire-pixel counts) as an instrument for pollution to address measurement error.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control

Treatment variable  
• Core binary version: Region i is “treated” if the jump in PM2.5 (satellite-derived) between 1996 and 1997 is above the national median.  
  Treatment_i = 1{ΔPM_i,1997 ≥ median(ΔPM)}.  
• Preferred continuous version: ΔPM_it – the change in log(PM2.5) relative to 1996.

Control group  
• Regions whose 1997 pollution increase is below the median (or below the 25th percentile in stricter robustness) serve as controls.

Treatment timing  
• Post_t = 1 for years ≥ 1997. Pre-period = 1994-1996; post-period = 1997-2000 (or farther if data allow).

No RDD, so no running variable / cutoff applicable.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions

A1. Parallel Trends  
Absent the wildfires, mortality trends in high- and low-exposure regions would have evolved in parallel.

Plausibility: Infant mortality was falling fairly smoothly nation-wide in the early 1990s, and fire incidence in 1997 is largely weather-driven. We will test with pre-period event-study coefficients.

A2. No Differential Concurrent Shocks  
No other shock in 1997 affected mortality in high-exposure regions differently from low-exposure regions.

Plausibility: The Asian Financial Crisis hit the entire country, but heterogeneity in crisis intensity might correlate with fire locations. We will add controls for regional GDP, rice prices, and health spending.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers)  
Pollution generated in one region does not significantly alter mortality in control regions.

Plausibility: Haze traveled long distances; we therefore define regions using meteorological basins and test down-wind spillovers, dropping neighboring controls in robustness.

A4. No Sorting / Migration  
Families did not selectively migrate across regions in response to very rapid, unanticipated pollution changes.

Plausibility: Few households moved during the 3-4 month fire episode; birth cohorts can be assigned using mother’s residence at delivery. We show stable population counts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation

T1. Differential Economic Collapse (1997-98 crisis)  
Mitigation: control for regional GDP per capita, unemployment, and include region-specific linear trends; placebo test on 1995 bank-panic dummy.

T2. Measurement Error in Satellite PM  
Mitigation: use multiple pollution measures (PM2.5, Aerosol Optical Depth, fire counts); employ wildfire pixel count interacted with wind direction as an IV for PM.

T3. Pollution Spillovers / Mis-classification of Controls  
Mitigation: redefine exposure using inverse-distance weighted haze to get continuous treatment; drop regions within 300 km of treatment regions (“donut”); show robustness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline

```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional fixed effects
library(did2s)       # event study with Gardner (2022) dID
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# 1. Load data
d <- fread("indonesia_airhealth_1994_2000.csv")   # one row = region-year

# 2. Variable construction
# Pollution
d[, pm_log := log(pm25 + 0.1)]
d[, delta_pm96_97 := pm_log[year==1997] - pm_log[year==1996], by = region]

# Binary treatment defined once
median_jump <- median(d[year==1997, delta_pm96_97], na.rm=TRUE)
d[, treated := (delta_pm96_97 >= median_jump)[1], by = region]

# Post dummy
d[, post := as.integer(year >= 1997)]

# DID interaction
d[, treat_post := treated * post]

# Infant mortality (per 1,000 live births) – outcome
d[, imr := infant_deaths / live_births * 1000]

# 3. Main DID regression
did_main <- feols(imr ~ treat_post + gdp_pc + health_spend |
                  region + year, data = d, cluster = "region")
summary(did_main)

# 4. Event-study (Sun & Abraham staggered adoption = identical timing here, but good for leads/lags)
d[, rel_year := year - 1997]
event <- feols(imr ~ i(rel_year, treated, ref = -1) + gdp_pc + health_spend |
               region + year, data = d, cluster = "region")
iplot(event, ci = TRUE, ref.line = 0)

# 5. Robustness: continuous treatment intensity
d[, pm_change := pm_log - pm_log[year==1996], by = region]
did_cont <- feols(imr ~ pm_change*post + gdp_pc |
                  region + year, data = d, cluster = "region")
summary(did_cont)
```

Optional IV robustness:  

```r
library(ivreg)
iv <- feols(imr ~ (pm_change*post) | region + year |
            . ~ fire_pixel_count*post, data = d, cluster = "region")
summary(iv)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results

Direction: Higher particulate exposure raises early-life mortality.  
Magnitude: Literature (e.g., Currie et al.) suggests a 10 µg/m³ increase in PM2.5 raises neonatal mortality by ≈1–3%. Indonesia’s fires raised PM by >100 µg/m³ in some regions, so we expect a 10–30% increase in infant mortality in the most polluted areas, translating into roughly 5–10 additional deaths per 1,000 live births.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)

C1: Pre-trends (parallel) visually and statistically confirmed …………………. 1  
C2: No concurrent shocks differentially hitting treatment regions ……………… 0  
C3: No anticipation of treatment ………………………………………………………… 1  
C4: Stable composition (no selective migration, fertility) ……………………… 0  
C5: No spillovers or interference across units ……………………………………… 0  

Total = 2 / 5. We therefore put special effort into robustness checks for C2–C5 and will transparently report any residual concerns.
